`set -u` only catches UNDEFINED variables, not empty strings:

```sh

VAR="${INPUT:-}"; echo ${VAR}  # OK - always defined
```

ideas.rule: When a PR extracts guidance out of one artifact into a new one, the extracted content must be reconciled against the artifacts that already exist -- the extraction itself is not evidence of de-duplication.
ideas.why: This PR's stated goal was to eliminate duplication ("ensures all AI agents use the same guidelines without duplication"), and it did remove the .cursorrules/AGENTS.md pair -- but it moved the payload into a new file that collides with, and in two places contradicts, .claude/docs/WORKFLOWS.md. Nothing in the current checklists asks a reviewer to diff a newly-extracted doc against its siblings, so a consolidation PR can plausibly increase net contradiction while appearing to reduce it. This would fire on any repo that grows a standards-doc directory incrementally.

ideas.rule: A context file must not grow a new top-level topic when it already links a standards doc that owns that topic; new detail belongs in the linked doc.
ideas.why: CF01 catches the size symptom and CF05 catches the precedence symptom, but neither states the positive rule that drives both: growth in a hub file should be routed to the spoke. This is the single most common way an AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md drifts over budget one well-intentioned PR at a time, and it is mechanically checkable — a new `###` section whose heading matches a heading in a doc the file already links.

ideas.rule: A context file that pulls in another document (an `@path` import, an include, or a link presented as auto-loaded) must reference a path that exists in the repository; when the target is deliberately optional or gitignored, the file must say so on the same line.
ideas.why: no-broken-links-SK13 covers this for skills only — no context-file check verifies that an import resolves. Here CLAUDE.md gains a bare `@AGENTS.local.md` sitting in an otherwise uniform list of eight real `@.claude/docs/*.md` imports, and the target is gitignored and absent from the repo. A reader or a linter cannot distinguish 'intentionally optional' from 'someone deleted the file', and the identical check would fire in any repo using @-imports.

ideas.rule: A context file must not import an untracked, machine-local document without bounding what that document may override.
ideas.why: Nothing in the catalog scores the trust boundary of a context file's imports. An unbounded local override means the effective instruction set differs per developer and per CI machine, and reviewers reading the committed artifact cannot see what an agent actually loaded — a reproducibility problem that generalizes to every harness supporting local overrides.

ideas.rule: An `@`-import in a context file must point at a path that is guaranteed to resolve; if the target is optional or gitignored, the file must name the exact path in prose so the agent can read it manually rather than silently loading nothing.
ideas.why: Nothing in context-file-checklist.md checks import resolution, and `no-broken-links-SK13` is scoped to skills only. A silently-failing `@`-import is invisible: the agent produces a normal-looking turn with a whole tier of local guidance missing. This PR is a maintainer fixing exactly that failure by hand, which is evidence the class is real and recurring, and it would fire in any repo using `@`-import context files.

ideas.rule: A standards doc should not end with a summary/'key principles' section that restates rules already stated in its body; a rule must have exactly one home inside the file it lives in.
ideas.why: no-duplication-GR01 is written as a cross-file check ('already exists elsewhere'), so intra-file restatement currently only lands under the weaker concise-GR03. Self-duplication is a distinct and very common LLM-authored-doc defect: it doubles token cost and guarantees the two copies drift apart on the next edit.

ideas.rule: A context file's `@path` imports are inlined into every turn, not loaded on demand — count imported files against the context file's token budget and flag an import whose target is itself over budget.
ideas.why: CF01 measures only the context file's own body, so a CLAUDE.md can stay 'lean' on paper while @-importing six documents that together add ten thousand tokens to every turn. Nothing in the current catalog distinguishes a link (progressive disclosure) from an @-import (unconditional inlining), yet they have opposite cost profiles. Mechanically checkable from the import list.

ideas.rule: A fenced code block nested inside another fenced block must use more backticks on the outer fence; equal-length fences terminate early and truncate the rendered example.
ideas.why: Skills get `clean-structure-SK14` ('closed code fences') but standards docs get no equivalent, and a broken fence silently swallows the rest of a section for the model reading it. Trivially checkable and applies to any artifact type that carries examples.

ideas.rule: When an artifact file is a symlink (git mode 120000), grade it once through its target and never as an independent document; a review that opens both names will double-count every guideline the target contains.
ideas.why: No checklist mentions symlinked artifacts, yet multi-harness repos increasingly ship CLAUDE.md/.cursorrules/AGENTS.md as symlinks to one real file. Without an explicit rule, no-duplication-GR01 fires spuriously on every symlink pair and token budgets are counted twice.

ideas.rule: A PR that only changes which of two symlinked names holds the bytes must be verified as content-neutral by comparing blob hashes, not by reading the +/- line counts.
ideas.why: A pure symlink swap presents as a large +219/-219 diff and looks like a substantive rewrite to any reviewer or tool reading line counts. A generic check that a rename/swap is byte-identical would prevent both false positives and, more importantly, catch the case where a maintainer smuggles content edits into a 'swap' commit.
ideas.grounded_in: AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md — both sides of the swap resolve to blob 2c055551ed4

ideas.rule: A skill invoked non-interactively (from CI, a cron job, or a workflow file) must state its non-interactive contract: what it does when required input is missing, and what its terminal output must look like for the caller to parse.
ideas.why: skill-checklist.md's Workflows section assumes a human is watching — observable steps, reviewer in the loop. It has no check for the growing class of skills whose only caller is a YAML workflow, where a skill that silently produces nothing is indistinguishable from one that found nothing. This would fire on any repo that wires skills into CI.
ideas.grounded_in: .claude/skills/doc-check/SKILL.md:31 ('Report findings - Use the method provided in the prompt, or if none specified, summarize findings directly')

ideas.rule: A skill that tells the agent to consult another artifact ("check AGENTS.md first") must not also restate that artifact's content; flag any skill that both cites a context file as authoritative and duplicates a section from it.
ideas.why: This is a sharper, mechanically detectable special case of no-duplication-GR01: the skill has already named its own source of truth, so the duplication is self-evidently unnecessary and the conflict-resolution order is ambiguous the moment either copy drifts. GR01 catches the duplication but not the self-contradiction, which is the part a reviewer can point at without any repo-wide grep.
ideas.grounded_in: .claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md:43 ("check AGENTS.md first") vs :50 and :60 (AGENTS.md content restated)

ideas.rule: A skill that defines a severity or classification taxonomy must state what the agent does with each level (post, summarize, suppress), not just name the levels.
ideas.why: Taxonomies with no downstream behavior are decorative token spend. This skill defines CRITICAL/IMPORTANT/NITPICK and never says whether a NITPICK should be posted at all, while a later section says not to comment below 80% confidence — leaving the two rules unreconciled. Applies to any review, triage, or audit skill in any repo.

ideas.rule: A rename or path migration of a context file must be reviewed for the content it carries, not waved through as a move; treat any line that differs from the source file as a normal added guideline.
ideas.why: Git renders this PR as a 129-line delete plus a 130-line add, which reads as a large new artifact, while the actual authoring decision is a single new bullet. A reviewer who trusts the file-status metadata either over-files (grading 130 pre-existing lines as new) or under-files (dismissing the whole PR as a move). A check that says 'diff renamed artifacts against their predecessor before scoring' would prevent both, and this failure mode recurs on every AGENTS.md migration.

ideas.rule: A standards doc pulled into a context file via an always-on include directive (`@path`) should be held to the context file's token budget, not treated as on-demand reference material.
ideas.why: standards-checklist.md has no size check at all, on the assumption that a standards doc loads only when relevant. AGENTS.md here @-includes eight docs unconditionally; GO.md alone is ~3,453 tokens, so a single line in a context file quietly added more than the entire 2,000-token context-file budget to every turn. The distinction between a linked doc and an @-included doc is invisible to every current check and generalizes to any repo using include directives.

ideas.rule: Guidance keyed to a tool or language version must state where the authoritative version comes from and must not present rules the project cannot yet use as if they were current.
ideas.why: GO.md is a good-faith example of getting this right — it has a 'Since' column and a 'Version misuse' pitfall — which is exactly why it shows the check is expressible. Nothing in standards-checklist.md requires it, so a version-keyed doc without those guards would pass today and silently instruct the agent to emit code that does not compile.

ideas.rule: A command introduced in a context file's command table must not be re-explained as a prose section in the same file; the table entry should carry the one-line semantics, or the prose section should own it, but not both.
ideas.why: GR01 is scoped to advice that exists *elsewhere*, so it does not cleanly fire when a single PR creates both copies inside one file. Command-table-plus-prose-section is a recurring context-file shape, and the two copies drift independently — the table's Notes column and the section's bullet list are updated by different PRs. A check that a context file states each command's semantics exactly once would fire on this shape in any repo.
ideas.grounded_in: AGENTS.md:53-54 (`make pre-commit` / `make pre-push` table rows) vs AGENTS.md:113-116 (the same two commands re-explained in the Git Hooks section)

ideas.rule: A build/test command table should have exactly one canonical home; other artifacts link to it rather than restating the commands.
ideas.why: Nothing in standards-checklist.md or context-file-checklist.md checks for a command table replicated across containers, and GR01 is awkward to apply to a cheatsheet where repetition looks conventional. The cost is only visible on maintenance: removing one defunct make target here required coordinated edits in four separate artifact files, and any one of them could have been missed, leaving an agent with a command that fails. A check that fires when the same command table appears in more than one artifact would generalize to every repo with both a context file and standards docs.

ideas.rule: When a context file already links or @-imports a dedicated standards doc for a domain, new advice in that domain must go into the linked doc rather than being appended inline to the context file.
ideas.why: The 'right home' guideline check is generic and does not know about a repo's own doc topology. A mechanical version — 'this context file imports DATABASE.md; your new bullet is about database queries' — would fire reliably and is checkable from the import list plus the section heading.

ideas.rule: Every relative link in a standards doc must resolve from that doc's own directory, not from the repository root.
ideas.why: standards-checklist.md has no link-integrity check at all — `no-broken-links-SK13` exists only for skills, so a standards doc can ship a dead pointer and no code in the catalog can be cited. This PR introduces three of them in one commit: `.claude/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `PR_STYLE_GUIDE.md`, and `WORKFLOWS.md` each link `[CONTRIBUTING.md](docs/about/contributing/CONTRIBUTING.md#commit-messages)`, which resolves relative to `.claude/docs/` and points at the non-existent `.claude/docs/docs/about/contributing/CONTRIBUTING.md`. The correct target is `../../docs/about/contributing/CONTRIBUTING.md`. This is the highest-value gap I hit in this batch: the whole consolidation strategy of the PR rests on those three links, and all three are dead.

ideas.rule: When a guideline points at a canonical doc for the full rules, it should not also restate those rules inline — link or state, not both.
ideas.why: no-duplication-GR01 catches the copy-vs-copy case but says nothing about the link-plus-restatement pattern, which is how consolidation PRs silently reintroduce the drift they set out to remove. A check for 'this line says See X for full rules and then enumerates the rules anyway' would fire in any repo that maintains a docs hub.

ideas.rule: Guidance harvested from past code-review comments should be filed by domain into the doc that owns the domain, not appended wholesale to the nearest context file — flag a single diff that adds three or more new top-level topic sections to a context file.
ideas.why: 'Lessons learned from review' PRs are a recurring artifact genre and they systematically bloat context files, because appending is the path of least resistance. Section-count delta on a context file is a cheap mechanical signal that generalises to any repo.

ideas.rule: When a skill names another document as the canonical authority for a topic, it must not also restate individual rules from that document; it should link and stop.
ideas.why: GR01 catches the duplicate only if the reviewer happens to grep the right file. A dedicated check keyed on the skill's own 'canonical docs' / 'References' section would make the failure mechanical: any rule in the skill body that also appears in a doc the skill declares canonical is by construction a drift hazard. This pattern — a References section that defers, followed by a rules section that re-implements — is common enough to be worth checking on every skill.
ideas.grounded_in: .agents/skills/pull-requests/SKILL.md:20-24 (References section naming PR_STYLE_GUIDE.md canonical) vs :38 (restating its draft rule)

ideas.rule: A guideline scoped to specific directories should name the mechanism that keeps its scope accurate, or the scope silently rots as directories are added, renamed, or opted in.
ideas.why: Path-scoped advice is a growing category — compiler opt-ins, strict-mode islands, migration boundaries — and it has a failure mode plain guidelines do not: the rule stays literally true while becoming materially wrong, because a third directory joined the opt-in and nobody updated the prose. Unlike a stale general rule, this one gives no signal when it drifts. A check that path-scoped guidance either derives its scope from config or names where the authoritative list lives would apply in any repo doing incremental migration.
ideas.grounded_in: site/AGENTS.md:161-162, which hardcodes `src/pages/AgentsPage/` and `src/components/ai-elements/` as the React Compiler opt-in set

ideas.rule: An artifact must not hardcode a specific model name, model version, or vendor tool name in content that is meant to apply to any agent (attribution footers, commit trailers, prompt templates). Name the capability, or let the running agent supply its own identity.
ideas.why: This PR exists solely because .claude/docs/PR_STYLE_GUIDE.md told every agent to sign PRs as 'Claude Sonnet 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>' via 'Claude Code'. That went stale silently and became actively wrong once Coder Agents and other tools started opening PRs. No check in standards-checklist.md, skill-checklist.md, or context-file-checklist.md catches a hardcoded model/vendor string. It is mechanically greppable (model-version patterns, vendor names in template blocks) and would fire in essentially every repo in this benchmark.

ideas.rule: When a context file restates its own `@`-import list as manual prose for harnesses that do not auto-load imports, the two lists must be marked as mirrors of each other so a later PR that adds a doc to one is forced to update the other.
ideas.why: Multi-harness repos increasingly carry the same reference list twice — once as `@path` imports for Claude Code, once as a prose 'read these manually' list for everything else. Nothing in the checklists notices that these are duplicate lists with a drift hazard, and no-duplication-GR01 cannot fire because the duplication is deliberate. A check for 'harness-conditional mirror lists are marked and equal in membership' would fire in any repo that supports more than one agent runtime, and it is mechanically verifiable: the set of `@`-referenced paths should equal the set of paths in the manual list.
ideas.grounded_in: AGENTS.md:290-298 (the `@.claude/docs/*.md` import block) vs AGENTS.md:300-318 (the manual read list added by this PR)

ideas.rule: A conditional-loading list should state its trigger per entry, not just per group; 'read when relevant to your task' is unactionable without a concrete condition attached to each item.
ideas.why: Progressive disclosure only works if the agent can decide, cheaply and correctly, whether to load a given file. Grouping a dozen docs under one vague heading pushes that decision back onto the model. This PR actually does it right — every entry carries a parenthetical trigger — which is exactly what makes it a good positive exemplar for a check that would fail the far more common version of this list, where entries are bare filenames. Applicable to any context file or skill that enumerates on-demand references.
ideas.grounded_in: AGENTS.md:308-315, e.g. "`.claude/docs/GO.md` — Go patterns and modern Go usage (any Go changes)"

ideas.rule: A heading or bolded lead-in that introduces content must be followed by that content — flag dangling section headers whose body is empty.
ideas.why: SKILL.md line 62 reads '**Write descriptive test cases:**' and is followed by a blank line and then an unrelated bolded sentence; the promised examples never appear. clean-structure-SK14 covers closed fences, orphaned files and duplicated content but has no check for a header that promises content it does not deliver, which is a common symptom of a truncated or hand-merged skill.

ideas.rule: A skill that prescribes a methodology (TDD, trunk-based development, a specific review flow) must state the classes of change it does not apply to.
ideas.why: A methodology skill with no stated non-applicability will be applied to trivial changes, which is where over-rigid workflow skills do the most damage. honest-scope-SK07 asks a skill to say when *not* to use it only when it overlaps a sibling skill; there is no check for a skill that overreaches its own subject matter.

ideas.rule: A role/persona prompt file that a skill spawns as a subagent should declare its scope boundary and its output contract (where it writes, what format), and the spawning skill's prompt template must actually pass those variables.
ideas.why: subagent-checklist.md is a stub, and these files are subagents in everything but path — they live under a skill root, so skill-checklist.md grades the container and nothing grades the persona. deep-review does this well (every roles/*.md ends with a 'Scope boundaries' line and the Tier-1/Tier-2 prompts pass an output file), which makes it a good positive template for the missing checklist.

ideas.rule: When a skill hard-codes an output directory under /tmp, it must define collision behavior and retention, not just create the path.
ideas.why: Nothing in skill-checklist.md covers durable-artifact location quality — SK19 asks only that progress artifacts exist. A timestamp-seeded /tmp path is invisible to the repo, unrecoverable after a reboot, and cannot be attached to the PR, yet it is the sole channel between fourteen subagents and the orchestrator.

ideas.rule: A skill reference doc that restates general ecosystem knowledge must state its precedence relative to the repo's own context files, or scope itself to 'unless the project says otherwise'.
ideas.why: standards-checklist.md has stated-precedence-SD01, but it applies only to freestanding standards docs. A reference doc living under a skill's references/ gets no precedence check at all, even though it is loaded into a subagent's context exactly like a standards doc. This PR added 16.5k tokens of general React/TypeScript guidance that silently competes with repo-specific rules in site/AGENTS.md, with nothing declaring a winner. The defect generalizes to any repo that pairs a vendored-style language reference with a local context file.

ideas.rule: When a skill adds a reference doc, the marginal expanded-context cost should be stated and bounded relative to the number of subagents that will load it.
ideas.why: checked-token-cost-SK25 asks that references be 'genuinely on-demand', which these are, but it has no notion of fan-out. deep-review spawns one Modernization Reviewer instance per language, and a .tsx-heavy diff spawns both, so this PR's two references cost ~16.5k tokens per review run rather than the ~8k a single load suggests. A check that multiplies reference size by the skill's declared parallelism would catch a cost class SK25 currently reports as zero.

ideas.rule: A skill that defines a classification vocabulary (severity levels, finding categories, status labels) must apply every downstream gate to every member of that vocabulary, or state explicitly which members are exempt and why.
ideas.why: This is a real, shipped defect class that no current check reaches: deep-review defined an 'Obs' tier alongside P1-P4 but routed only 'findings' through the severity test, so anything filed as an observation silently bypassed both the upgrade check and the novelty gate. The gap is mechanically visible — enumerate the terms the skill defines, then check each one appears in the gating steps — and it generalises to any skill with a taxonomy.

ideas.rule: Advice that hard-codes a source directory path must be verifiable against the tree at review time; prefer naming the owning module or a glob over an exact folder path that a refactor will silently invalidate.
ideas.why: Nothing in context-file-checklist.md or guideline-rule-checklist.md checks that a path named inside an advice line still resolves. This PR exists only because a folder move stranded the path list in an AGENTS.md advice line; had the artifact not been updated in the same PR, the guidance would have silently pointed at a directory that no longer exists and the React Compiler rule would have applied to nothing. SK13 covers relative links in skills but there is no equivalent for source paths cited inside advice in any container.

ideas.rule: A guideline that names a specific source-file path as the subject of a rule must be verifiable: the named path has to exist at review time, and the rule should say what happens when the file is renamed, split, or deleted.
ideas.why: File-scoped exception rules ('handlers in coderd/exp_chats.go omit swagger annotations') go stale silently. The file gets renamed or the pattern spreads to a sibling, and the artifact keeps steering the agent with a rule that no longer maps to anything. Nothing in guideline-rule-checklist.md or context-file-checklist.md checks that a cited source path resolves — SK13 only covers paths named inside a skill. This is mechanically checkable in any repo and would fire on artifacts nobody has seen yet.

ideas.rule: A nested AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md should declare its relationship to the root context file — what it overrides, what it inherits — rather than silently re-deriving repo-wide rules.
ideas.why: context-file-checklist.md has no check for the root-vs-nested relationship. aibridge/AGENTS.md was written as if the repo had no root context file, which is how the time.Sleep and Uber-style-guide duplications got in. This generalizes: any repo with more than one context file has this failure mode.

ideas.rule: A Markdown table used to carry guidance must be structurally valid: every row's cell count matches the header, and any literal pipe inside a cell is escaped.
ideas.why: This PR exists because one unescaped pipe inside a regex example ('/[.\*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g') split a row into an extra column, which silently shifted the 'Modern replacement' advice into the 'Since' column and appended a phantom fourth column to the separator row for the whole table. The agent reading that file was being handed a corrupted rule, and nothing in guideline-rule-checklist.md, standards-checklist.md, or skill-checklist.md catches it — SK14 covers unclosed code fences but not malformed tables. This is trivially checkable, it is a real observed corruption rather than a hypothetical, and tables are a common guidance container in every repo.

ideas.rule: A context file that maintains a navigation index into dedicated standards docs should route new domain-specific advice into the indexed doc rather than appending a new inline section; flag any added section whose topic matches an already-linked doc's domain.
ideas.why: AGENTS.md here is explicitly a hub with an 'Agent navigation' index into eleven .claude/docs/* standards docs, yet successive PRs keep appending topic sections (API Design, Database Query Naming, Database-to-SDK Conversions, Transactions and InTx) inline. No current check compares an added heading against the domains of the docs the same file already links to, so the hub silently accretes into the thing it was designed to avoid. This is mechanically checkable and would fire across any repo using the hub-plus-standards-docs pattern.
ideas.grounded_in: AGENTS.md:11 (navigation link to .claude/docs/DATABASE.md) vs AGENTS.md:131 (new inline '### Transactions and `InTx`' section)

ideas.rule: When a change adds a prose guideline and an automated enforcement mechanism for that same guideline in the same commit, the prose should be reduced to a pointer at the check (its command and its failure message) rather than a full restatement of the rule.
ideas.why: not-lintable-GR02 catches 'this could be linted' but has nothing to say about the strictly worse case where the author has already written the linter and then also writes the rule out longhand in three files. That is the pattern here: scripts/check_emdash.sh plus `make lint/emdash` plus 28 lines of prose across three artifacts. A check phrased as 'guideline added alongside its own enforcement' is mechanically detectable from a diff and would generalise to any repo that lints its conventions.
ideas.grounded_in: AGENTS.md:289-303 together with scripts/check_emdash.sh and the Makefile lint/emdash target, all added in this commit

ideas.rule: A guideline about an external surface the repo does not own (a PR body, a commit message, a Slack post, an issue template) must say so explicitly, so it is not applied to committed files that carry contrary formatting rules.
ideas.why: This PR exists precisely because that ambiguity bit: the repo's AGENTS.md tells agents to wrap comment lines at 80 columns, and an agent generalised that to GitHub PR descriptions, where hard wrapping renders badly. The fix was to add a scoping sentence ('Committed Markdown and code comments may have their own formatting rules. Do not apply those wrapping rules to PR descriptions.'). Nothing in guideline-rule-checklist.md or standards-checklist.md asks whether a rule names its surface — GR04 covers where the rule LIVES, not what it APPLIES to. Repo-external surfaces are common (commit messages, PR bodies, release notes) and unreachable by linters, so mis-scoped advice there is both frequent and undetectable by tooling.

ideas.rule: A context file should expose one routing surface, not several; adding a second navigation block while an existing one remains is a defect even when both lists are individually correct.
ideas.why: Nothing in context-file-checklist.md scores routing-surface count. CF02 governs topic length and CF05 governs precedence, but neither notices a file that grew a second table of contents. This is a recurring shape in artifact repos: a doc-hub refactor adds a fresh navigation block at the top and leaves the old one at the bottom, and the two drift within a release. Mechanically detectable as two or more blocks linking the same set of paths.
ideas.grounded_in: AGENTS.md:6-14 (new '## Agent navigation') versus AGENTS.md:196-207 ('Documentation Guide')

ideas.rule: A doc that cites the canonical location for a rule should defer to it rather than restating the rule underneath the citation.
ideas.why: AGENT_FAILURES.md gives every entry an explicit 'Existing docs or tools' field and then a 'Proposed prevention' field that re-states what those docs say. GR01 catches the duplication only if a reviewer thinks to grep; a check aimed at the link-then-restate shape would catch it structurally and would generalise to any repo running a docs hub. Same shape seen independently in PR 23096 in this batch, which raises my confidence it is a real recurring pattern rather than one author's habit.

ideas.rule: When a PR creates several standards docs at once, each must declare a non-overlapping domain, and any topic claimed by two of them is a finding at creation time.
ideas.why: SD02 grades one file in isolation and SD03 only checks shadowing by a *skill*, so a commit that lands three sibling docs with overlapping remits (OBSERVABILITY.md's failure playbooks versus AGENT_FAILURES.md's catalog) passes every existing check. Creation time is the only cheap moment to fix it.

ideas.rule: A nested context file that declares a parent file authoritative for a topic must not restate advice on that topic; the declaration and the content have to agree.
ideas.why: CF05 (defers on conflict) checks that a deferral statement exists, and GR01 checks for duplication, but nothing checks the two against each other. A file that says 'root owns testing patterns' and then ships three testing rules is a specific, mechanically detectable inconsistency — match declared-deferral topics against the file's own section headings — and it is the characteristic failure mode of exactly this kind of monorepo-absorption cleanup.

ideas.rule: When a new guideline line restates the rationale of an adjacent existing line, it should extend that line rather than sit beside it as a separate bullet.
ideas.why: no-duplication-GR01 only catches a genuinely duplicated or conflicting instruction, so a rule that shares a premise with its neighbour but states a different consequence passes today. The result is a list that grows one bullet per bug fixed, each re-teaching the same fact — the mechanism by which context files drift over budget. Distinct from GR01 because neither line is redundant on its own; the defect is placement.

ideas.rule: A shared-repo artifact must not hard-code an individual person's name, handle, or a personal attribution string as required output text.
ideas.why: This skill instructs every agent that loads it to post the literal line '> Mux is acting on Mike's behalf.' on pull requests. A named individual baked into a repo-wide artifact is wrong for every other contributor who triggers the skill, and it goes stale the moment that person leaves. Nothing in skill-checklist.md covers personal identifiers — SK14 catches absolute user paths and stale model names but not hard-coded human attribution. Mechanically checkable and would fire in any repository.

ideas.rule: A skill that instructs the agent to poll or wait must bound the wait, or state explicitly what the agent should report and hand back when the bound is reached.
ideas.why: Line 47 says 'Wait indefinitely for the app's first response after each request' and line 268 says 'Do not replace waiting with a timeout.' An unbounded poll loop inside an agent turn burns tokens and wall-clock with no escape hatch and no user-visible checkpoint. skill-checklist.md's workflow checks cover tracking (SK16), observability (SK17), and progress artifacts (SK19), but none of them says a wait must terminate. This recurs in any skill that waits on CI, a deploy, or an external reviewer.

ideas.rule: A guideline added to an always-loaded context file at the same time as a repo-wide mechanical sweep enforcing it should state whether a linter/formatter rule was considered and why it was not used.
ideas.why: not-lintable-GR02 fires on the guideline but has no way to distinguish 'no tool can do this' from 'nobody checked'. A codemod-shaped PR (many files, one-line identical change each) is a strong, mechanically detectable signal that the rule is automatable, and it is exactly the moment the author has the evidence to decide. No current check reads that signal.
ideas.grounded_in: site/AGENTS.md:104 (added alongside identical one-line edits across 17 site/src files in the same commit)

ideas.rule: When advice is deliberately duplicated for proximity ('the canonical doc is too long to be read at the moment of use'), the copy must be marked as a mirror of a named source rather than restated as an independent rule.
ideas.why: no-duplication-GR01 is binary today, so an author with a legitimate proximity motive has no compliant option and simply duplicates. A 'mirrored from X' convention keeps the check's teeth while giving the honest case somewhere to go, and it makes drift detectable later. This exact tension is stated openly in the PR description.

ideas.rule: If a skill's stated reason for inlining content is that the referenced doc is too long to be found in time, the finding belongs against the referenced doc's length, not the skill.
ideas.why: The catalog can flag the duplicate but cannot express 'the root cause is a 200-line standards doc with no summary section'. A check that follows the citation and measures the target would catch a failure mode that currently gets fixed by copy-paste in every repo.

ideas.rule: When a standards doc declares an entry template in its own preamble, every entry must fill every declared field with substantive content — a field present but answered with a restatement of the symptom is a silent template violation.
ideas.why: one-topic-per-file-SD02 and every-line-scored-SD05 grade domain and advice quality, but nothing checks a doc against a schema the doc itself publishes. Template-structured catalogs (failure catalogs, ADR logs, runbook indexes) are common and degrade in a specific way: contributors keep the headings and hollow out the fields, so the structure still looks healthy while the content stops being actionable. Mechanically checkable wherever a doc shows a fenced template followed by repeated instances of it.

ideas.rule: An MCP server entry whose transport requires an already-running local process (type `http`/`sse` pointing at localhost) must document the start command, or the config should use a stdio entry that launches it; a bare localhost URL fails silently as a connection error the agent cannot diagnose.
ideas.why: other-checklist.md is a stub, so nothing today catches an MCP entry that is unreachable by default. The failure mode is uniquely bad: the client reports a connection refusal with no hint that a `pnpm storybook` process was the missing precondition. This repo handled it correctly by documenting the start command in site/AGENTS.md, which is exactly the pattern a check should require rather than leave to authorial diligence. Generalizes to any repo declaring a local HTTP MCP server.

ideas.rule: MCP server commands must pin the versions of remotely fetched executables rather than resolving `@latest` (or an unpinned tag) at every launch.
ideas.why: An unpinned `@latest` in an MCP command makes the agent's tool surface non-reproducible and turns any upstream release into an unreviewed change to the harness — the same supply-chain concern a lockfile exists to solve, but in a file no lockfile covers. Mechanically checkable from the args array and applicable to every repo with an .mcp.json.

ideas.rule: A settings/mcp file change should be reviewable as a semantic diff; flag PRs that reindent or reformat the whole file in the same commit as a functional entry, since the real change is hidden inside a whitespace-only rewrite.
ideas.why: This diff is +52/-35 for what is semantically a four-line addition, because the file was converted from spaces to tabs at the same time. Review attention is finite and this pattern reliably smuggles harness-permission changes past reviewers. Detectable by comparing the whitespace-normalized diff against the raw diff, and applies to settings.json, .mcp.json, and hook files in any harness.
ideas.grounded_in: .mcp.json:1-40 (entire file reindented from 2-space to tab in the same commit that adds the storybook entry)

ideas.rule: Advice must not be conditioned on a transitional state the agent cannot observe ("currently a scaffold", "until X lands", "for now"); state the rule that holds today and remove the conditional when the transition completes.
ideas.why: A pointer that says 'use B until A is populated' silently becomes wrong the moment A is populated, and nothing in the repo forces a revisit — the guidance decays without any diff. This is a whole class of self-invalidating instruction that no current code catches: SK14 mentions 'unmarked time-sensitive claims' but is scoped to skills only, and nothing equivalent exists for standards docs or context files. Mechanically detectable from phrasing, and it would fire in any repo mid-migration.
ideas.grounded_in: .claude/docs/DOCS_STYLE_GUIDE.md:14-16 ("That guide is currently a scaffold; continue using the **Writing Style** section below until it is populated.") and AGENTS.md:15

ideas.rule: When a PR narrows or transfers a standards doc's stated domain, every artifact that describes that doc's domain must be updated in the same change; flag a doc whose self-description no longer matches how its referrers describe it.
ideas.why: Precedence checks (SD01) verify a doc declares who wins, but nothing verifies that the declaration agrees with what the linking artifacts say the doc is for. Here DOCS_STYLE_GUIDE.md was rewritten to disclaim prose in the same commit that left AGENTS.md:12 asserting it owns prose. A referrer-consistency check is checkable from the link graph and generalizes to any repo with a context-file navigation index.

ideas.rule: A skill that names a canonical source doc for a topic must not then restate that doc's content in its own body — the reference and the restatement are a self-contradiction the reviewer can detect mechanically (link target + overlapping headings/tables).
ideas.why: no-duplication-GR01 catches the duplicated line, but the sharper, more automatable signal is structural: this skill has a '## References' section listing DEV_ISOLATION.md as canonical and then reproduces three of that doc's sections. A container-level check on 'links to X, duplicates X' would flag the whole design rather than line by line.

ideas.rule: A skill must not hardcode an individual person's name or identity into its instructions or output templates.
ideas.why: Nothing in the catalog covers personalization that silently breaks for every other user of the repo. Here the skill instructs the agent to post '> Mux working on Mike's behalf' into public PR comments; any teammate invoking the skill emits a false attribution.

ideas.rule: When a standards doc revises an existing rule, the reviewer should require that every other artifact repeating the superseded wording is updated in the same change — a stale copy is worse than no copy, because the agent may load either.
ideas.why: GR01 fires on the duplicate, but it does not express the temporal hazard that makes this case severe: the PR's whole purpose was to stop agents adding //nolint:testpackage, yet it left WORKFLOWS.md and TROUBLESHOOTING.md still teaching the old rule, so an agent loading those first learns the wrong thing. A 'supersession sweep' check would generalize to any repo with more than one guidance doc.

ideas.rule: A guideline that names the agent's own authoring process as its subject ('do not describe the reasoning the agent used to produce the change') should be scored for whether it survives the agent's absence — a rule aimed at one authoring tool's habits rather than at the code's readers dates out and is invisible to human contributors who never see the artifact.
ideas.why: guideline-rule-checklist.md scores duplication, lintability, concision, home, force, and phrasing, but has no check for whether a rule is about the code or about the model. Agent-directed meta-rules are a fast-growing class in AGENTS.md files and they leak authoring-tool state into what is nominally a code standard.

ideas.rule: A standards doc should not enumerate implementation details that the code owns (struct fields, log field names, route lists, env-var lists) without pointing at the source of truth; enumerate-and-link instead of enumerate-and-restate.
ideas.why: Nothing in standards-checklist.md checks whether a doc's factual claims about the codebase can go stale. This line is a hand-maintained mirror of the log fields emitted by coderd/httpmw/loggermw, and it only stayed accurate here because the PR author happened to remember to update it. Every subsequent field addition silently desyncs the agent's mental model. Mechanically checkable (a doc listing 5+ identifiers from one package should cite that package's path) and applies to any repo.

ideas.rule: When an artifact names another file as canonical and instructs the agent to read it first, it must not also restate that file's rules inline -- deference and restatement together guarantee drift.
ideas.why: No current check catches this shape. GR01 fires on the duplication, but the distinctive and more damaging pattern is the combination: a reader of the skill has no way to know which of the two copies is stale, and the explicit 'the content guidelines govern' sentence makes the inline copies look authoritative-by-association. This would fire on any repo that adopts a canonical-source model, which is an increasingly common artifact architecture.

ideas.rule: A guideline that cites the lint or CI command enforcing it should be a pointer to that command, not a restatement of the rule the command checks.
ideas.why: GR02 catches 'this could be automated'. It does not catch the narrower and more checkable case where the artifact itself names the automation and then duplicates its logic in prose anyway -- which is mechanically detectable (a guideline paragraph containing a command invocation plus an imperative rule) and is a reliable signal of redundant tokens.

ideas.rule: When a context file makes a document mandatory reading, that document must itself be graded as an artifact and counted against the agent's attention budget — regardless of whether its path sits under a harness root like .claude/ or .agents/.
ideas.why: The routing table classifies by path, so a 71 KB (~17,800 token) doc that AGENTS.md instructs the agent to consult before touching a subsystem falls through every checklist simply because it lives at coderd/x/chatd/ARCHITECTURE.md. That is a general and growing pattern — teams put agent-facing architecture docs next to the code — and today nothing scores them for length, precedence, or duplication.

ideas.rule: A context-file bullet that makes an agent responsible for keeping a document up to date should state the trigger condition concretely enough to be checkable, rather than relying on the agent's own judgement of what 'affects the architecture'.
ideas.why: covers-the-basics-CF04 and bounded-topics-CF02 both look at what a context file explains, but nothing scores the maintenance obligations it imposes. 'If you update the chatd subsystem in ways that affect the architecture, you must update the architecture document' is unfalsifiable in practice, so it will silently never fire — a general failure mode for 'keep the docs in sync' instructions.

ideas.rule: When a doc narrows its own declared scope, any section it just stopped claiming must be removed or explicitly re-pointed in the same change — a narrowed scope line plus an unrelocated section leaves orphaned guidance no rule now governs.
ideas.why: standards-checklist.md check 1 asks whether precedence is stated and check 3 whether a skill shadows the doc, but nothing catches the common migration shape where a doc hands a domain over to a new canonical location and leaves its old section behind. That orphan keeps loading and keeps competing, and it is invisible to a diff-level review because the offending content is on unchanged lines while the cause is on changed ones.
ideas.grounded_in: .claude/docs/DOCS_STYLE_GUIDE.md:13 (rewritten scope line) vs :139 ('## Writing Style', left in place)

ideas.rule: A relative link that includes a heading anchor (`path/to/doc.md#some-section`) must have the anchor verified, not just the file path.
ideas.why: skill-checklist.md check 13 verifies that relative paths exist, but says nothing about the fragment. This skill routes six of its eight canonical references through anchors, one of which is non-ASCII (`#follow-the-diátaxis-framework`) and therefore especially fragile to slugger differences and heading rewordings. A dead anchor silently dumps the agent at the top of a long document instead of on the rule it was sent to read — an artifact-wide failure mode that would fire in any repository practising progressive disclosure.

ideas.rule: When two skills form a deliberate pair, each one's description must state when NOT to use it and name the sibling that covers that case.
ideas.why: skill-checklist.md check 7 asks a skill to be 'distinct from sibling skills; states when *not* to use it if overlap is likely' but treats that as an aside inside honest-scope, and check 8 grades activation pull in isolation rather than against a competing skill. Here the pairing is handled well in prose, which shows the pattern is real and worth checking explicitly: paired skills are the most common source of mis-routing, and 'name your sibling and your non-trigger' is mechanically checkable across repos.
